course.title: Application Security (AppSec) — Complete Deep Security Course
course.description: A defensive, Application Security (AppSec)-specific course progressing from fundamentals to production security, with detailed explanations, safe practicals, dedicated tasks, security testing and a complete learning-platform capstone.
course.curriculumPolicy: Module and lesson counts are determined by the security concepts required to learn the discipline properly; no fixed cross-security template is imposed.
learningOutcomes: Identify assets, threats and trust boundaries.
Secure authentication, authorization and data flows.
Integrate security into development and operations.
Respond to and learn from security failures.

modules.title: AppSec Foundations
modules.description: Secure-by-design thinking, attack surface, security requirements and developer responsibility.

lessons.title: AppSec Foundations
lessons.description: Secure-by-design thinking, attack surface, security requirements and developer responsibility.
learningObjectives: Test normal and malicious/invalid cases safely.

notes.text: Secure-by-design thinking, attack surface, security requirements and developer responsibility.

Learn appsec foundations by first identifying the asset and trust boundary, then understanding the attack or failure mode, then applying a defense and finally testing that defense. The objective is defensive engineering, not memorizing isolated vulnerabilities.

AppSec Foundations is important because security failures often happen at boundaries between users, browsers, APIs, services, databases and deployment systems. Students should learn to prevent, detect and safely remediate these failures.

notes.alt: Application Security (AppSec) AppSec Foundations security diagram
notes.caption: Add a defensive architecture diagram showing the trust boundary, threat and mitigation for AppSec Foundations.

items: Identify the asset being protected.
Identify the trust boundary and attacker capability.
Understand the failure/vulnerability mechanism.
Apply layered defensive controls.
Create a test that proves the control works.

notes.code:
Scenario: Create security requirements for a new course feature.

Defensive workflow: identify the asset -> map the trust boundary -> define allowed behavior -> implement controls -> test negative cases -> monitor.

items: Locate the untrusted input or risky boundary.
Define what the application should allow.
Apply validation, authorization or isolation.
Verify the result with positive and negative tests.
Log the security-relevant event without exposing secrets.
Relying on client-side checks for security.
Using authentication without object-level authorization.
Logging passwords, tokens or sensitive personal data.
Fixing a symptom without identifying the trust boundary.
Skipping regression tests after a security fix.
Use defense in depth.
Enforce authorization on the server.
Keep secrets out of source code.
Prefer safe APIs and parameterized operations.
Automate security checks where practical.
Treat security findings as engineering work with owners and verification.
I can explain AppSec Foundations in my own words.
I can identify the affected trust boundary.
I can describe the defensive control.
I can create a negative test.
I can explain how the fix should be monitored.

Learn production appsec operations by first identifying the asset and trust boundary, then understanding the attack or failure mode, then applying a defense and finally testing that defense. The objective is defensive engineering, not memorizing isolated vulnerabilities.

Production AppSec Operations is important because security failures often happen at boundaries between users, browsers, APIs, services, databases and deployment systems. Students should learn to prevent, detect and safely remediate these failures.
